'''Square root biased sampling''' is a [[sampling (statistics)|sampling]] method proposed by [[William H. Press]], a [[computer scientist]] and [[computational biology|computational biologist]], for use in [[Airport security|airport screenings]]. It is the mathematically optimal compromise between [[Simple random sample|simple random sampling]] and [[Offender profiling|strong profiling]] that most quickly finds a rare malfeasor, given fixed screening resources.<ref name="the paper">{{Cite journal
  | last = Press
  | first = William H.
  | title = Strong profiling is not mathematically optimal for discovering rare malfeasors
  | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
  | volume = 106
  | issue = 6
  | pages = 1716–1719
  | date = February 10, 2009
  | doi = 10.1073/pnas.0813202106
  | pmc =2634801
  | pmid=19188610| doi-access = free
 | bibcode = 2009PNAS..106.1716P
 }}</ref><ref name="homeland" />

Using this method, if a group is <math alt="n">n</math> times as likely as the average to be a security risk, then persons from that group will be <math alt="square root of n">\sqrt{n}</math> times as likely to undergo [[Airport security#Process and equipment|additional screening]].<ref name="the paper" /> For example, if someone from a profiled group is nine times more likely than the average person to be a security risk, then when using [[square root]] biased sampling, people from the profiled group would be screened three times more often than the average person.

==History==
Press developed square root biased sampling as a way to sample long sequences of [[DNA]].<ref name="texas"/> It had also been developed independently by Ruben Abagyan, a professor at [[Scripps Research Institute|TSRI]] in La Jolla, California, for use in a different biological context.<ref>Abagyan RA, Totrov M (1999) "Ab initio folding of peptides by the optimal-bias Monte Carlo minimization procedure", Journal of Computational Physics, vol. 151, pp. 402-421.</ref><ref>Zhou Y, Abagyan R (2002) "Efficient stochastic global optimization for protein structure prediction", Rigidity  Theory and Applications, eds. Thorpe MF, Duxbury PM (New York, Springer).</ref> An even earlier discovery was by Martin L. Shooman, who used square root biased sampling in a test apportionment model for software reliability.<ref>M.L. Shooman, "A micro software reliability model for prediction and test apportionment," Proceedings 1991 International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (IEEE, 1991), pp. 52-59.</ref>

Press' later proposal to use square root biased sampling for airport security was published in 2009.<ref name="the paper"/> There, he argued that this method would be a more efficient use of the limited resources possessed for screening, as compared to the current practice, which can lead to screening the same persons frequently and repeatedly.<ref name="homeland">{{Cite news
  | title = Square root bias and airport security screening
  | newspaper = Homeland Security Newswire
  | date = 2009-02-03
  | url = http://homelandsecuritynewswire.com/square-root-bias-and-airport-security-screening
  | access-date = 2009-11-28
  }}</ref><ref name="texas">{{Cite news 
  | title = Researcher Proposes Statistical Method to Enhance Secondary Security Screenings
  | publisher = University of Texas at Austin News
  | date = 2009-02-03
  | url = http://www.utexas.edu/news/2009/02/03/statistical_security/
  | access-date = 2009-11-28}}
</ref> However, use of this method presupposes that those doing the screening have accurate [[statistical]] information on who is more likely to be a security risk, which is not necessarily the case.<ref>William Press, "To catch a terrorist: can ethnic profiling work?", Significance, December 2010, p. 164.</ref>
